notes.meaning: Moses promises that once the land of Canaan is conquered with the Lord's help, the two tribes will have met their duty. They will be free from any further obligation to the Lord and to the rest of Israel. Then the fertile land east of the Jordan will officially belong to them.

Moses warns them that breaking their promise is a direct sin against God, not just a failure toward their brothers. He tells them their sin will find them out, meaning the guilt and punishment of their wrongdoing will surely catch up with them. We cannot hide our disobedience from God, so we must turn from it before it brings ruin.

Moses tells the men to go ahead and repair towns for their children and pens for their flocks. At the same time, he insists that they must keep every word they spoke. Taking care of their families was necessary, but keeping their word to God and Israel was just as important.
The leaders of Gad and Reuben answer Moses with complete respect and submission. They agree to carry out every command their leader has laid down for them.

The two tribes lay out their battle plan clearly. Their wives, children, and livestock will remain behind safely in the fortified cities of Gilead. Meanwhile, every able-bodied warrior will cross over the Jordan River ready to fight for the Lord, exactly as Moses asked.

Moses knows he will die before Israel crosses the Jordan, so he entrusts the agreement to the next leaders. He charges Eleazar the high priest, Joshua, and the tribal heads to make sure the promises are kept.

Moses explains the first half of the agreement to the leaders. If the men of Gad and Reuben cross over armed and help conquer the land before the Lord, Israel must hand over Gilead as their permanent possession.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have argued that this chapter was put together from different written sources. They point to changes in wording, like "before Israel" and "before the LORD."

notes.meaning: Moses sets down the penalty if the two tribes break their word. If they refuse to cross over armed and fight beside the other tribes, they will lose their right to the land of Gilead. Instead, they will be forced to take whatever land is assigned to them across the river in Canaan.
The leaders of Gad and Reuben answer together as one voice. They accept Moses' terms and treat his words as a direct command from the Lord.
The two tribes repeat their vow with great firmness. They promise again to go over armed before the Lord into Canaan so that their requested inheritance east of the Jordan will truly become theirs.

Moses officially assigns the conquered lands of King Sihon and King Og to Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh. This grant includes all the towns and the regions around them. Half of Manasseh is added here because their clans helped fight and defeat the Amorites in northern Gilead.

The tribe of Gad restores and fortifies a series of captured towns, including Dibon and Aroer near the Arnon gorge. Because there was no time to construct brand new towns, they repaired existing walls to make safe homes for their families. They also built enclosed stone pens to protect their large flocks.

The tribe of Reuben rebuilds cities such as Heshbon, Elealeh, and Kiriathaim. They also repair Nebo and Baal-meon, changing their names to avoid honoring pagan idols. God's people were forbidden from calling upon false gods, so they gave the cities new Hebrew names.

The clan of Machir from the tribe of Manasseh attacks the northern area of Gilead, captures it, and drives out the Amorites living there. Their courage in battle won them the right to claim that rugged hill country.
Moses grants Gilead to the descendants of Machir because of their victory. The families of this clan settle down in the territory to make it their permanent homeland.
Jair, another brave warrior from the tribe of Manasseh, conquers a cluster of small rural villages in the region. He renames them Havvoth-jair, which means the tent-villages of Jair.

A leader named Nobah, also from Manasseh, captures the city of Kenath along with its surrounding settlements. He names the captured city Nobah after himself, though the older name was still remembered in later centuries.
